title.narrative: PNG-Australia Transport Sector Support Program (TSSP) Phase 3

description.narrative: Australia’s support to Papua New Guinea’s transport sector is delivered through the Transport Sector Support Program (TSSP). Commenced in 2007, TSSP is a multi-year commitment to support a more effective, efficient and inclusive transport system supporting PNG’s economic and social development. TSSP3 invests in quality transport infrastructure, capacity building and technical assistance for sector governance, strategic policy, as well as financial and procurement oversight for the program. Gender equity, disability inclusion and climate resilience are integrated throughout program delivery.

description.narrative: In 2024, TSSP3 commissioned the first-ever Market Analysis of PNG Road Contractors. The study surveyed 113 contractors across six provinces, finding 74 per cent of companies experienced growth in the past five years, largely due to access to donor and government-funded contracts. Notably, 58 per cent of surveyed contractors had previously delivered work under TSSP or similar donor-funded programs. ‍ Many contractors directly attributed business growth and job creation to participation in TSSP-funded projects, enabling expansion of operations, investment in equipment and hiring local staff. Respondents described TSSP as a critical enabler for securing work that would otherwise be inaccessible. For example, in Lae, a woman-led supply business used TSSP opportunities to grow her business and support her family. ‍ Several respondents highlighted that TSSP brought not only income but also skills development, with staff gaining technical and managerial experience. Regarding future support, contractors requested improved flexibility in rates, easier access to finance and insurance, more visibility on upcoming tenders, simplified procurement processes and enforcement of local content and anti-corruption policies. ‍ The analysis demonstrates that TSSP investments directly support economic participation, particularly in underserved and rural communities, underscoring its role in creating enabling conditions for long-term, inclusive growth in PNG’s infrastructure sector.

In 24/25, the journey to reshape PNG’s transport future took a major step forward. A TSSP3 technical adviser worked hand-in-hand with the Department of Transport to engage across the sector, aligning and refining priorities, culminating in the development of the Medium Term Transport Plan 3 (MTTP3) (2023-2027), which guides transport sector investment and reform across land, air and sea. MTTP3 was approved by the National Executive Council in June 2025 and reflects a whole-of-sector commitment to transparency, equity, environmental resilience and social inclusion. ‍ Designed to meet the Government’s requirement for alignment with the PNG Medium Term Development Plan IV (MTDP IV), MTTP3 focuses on five core goals: connecting communities through quality infrastructure, directing resources to the highest-impact projects, strengthening policy and regulation, enabling economic growth and extending the lifespan of existing assets through timely maintenance. ‍ MTTP3 includes the strategic framework, implementation roadmap and a new Monitoring, Reporting and Evaluation Framework (MREF). Replacing a patchwork of legacy systems, the MREF brings structure and clarity, reducing duplication, sharpening accountability and ensuring both infrastructure and policy initiatives are consistently measured. Together, these elements provide the foundation for a more connected, efficient and forward-looking transport sector.

The TSSP3 supported Milne Bay Long-Term Maintenance Contract (LTMC) maintains the 127km Magi Highway between Goilanai Bridge and Gadaisu, exemplifying G20-aligned quality infrastructure through strong governance, economic efficiency, environmental resilience and community benefit. ‍ The project incorporates joint quality assurance, social safeguards and community-responsive approaches, including subcontracting drainage works to local villagers to reduce disruptions in crop compensation zones. ‍ The LTMC model promotes lifecycle cost efficiency and sustainability by bundling rehabilitation and maintenance into a single contract, ensuring cost-effective delivery and sustained road quality across a critical regional network. ‍ The project has directly employed Papua New Guineans through a locally-owned company, creating an average of 87 jobs per month (76 men, 11 women), in both skilled and unskilled roles including road base preparation, drainage construction, sealing and safety upgrades like guardrails and line marking. To maintain progress, the contractor has increased the use of local labour. ‍ The LTMC model offers stability and skills development for workers, with involvement in advanced tasks such as bituminous sealing. This locally driven approach strengthens economic resilience, builds capacity and supports long-term development outcomes.

With TSSP3 support, the Department of Works and Highways (DoWH) developed the Climate Change Risk and Vulnerability Assessment (CCRVA) Framework. This was then piloted on two priority corridors: Magi Highway (Central Province) and the Lorengau to Momose Road (Manus Island). The pilots demonstrate strong alignment with G20 Principles for Quality Infrastructure Investment by embedding climate and disaster risk considerations into early-stage planning, design and decision-making. ‍ Applying an approved, structured four-stage process, the assessments identified and ranked vulnerable infrastructure assets based on exposure to climate hazards including extreme rainfall, sea-level rise and inland flooding. Standardised tools enabled consistent, geo-referenced data collection. Risk matrices prioritised adaptation measures, strengthened asset-level resilience and informed long-term planning. ‍ Beyond technical rigour, the pilots embedded inclusive engagement with provincial engineers and stakeholders, leveraging local knowledge of past climate impacts to shape context-appropriate solutions. Field-based assessments highlighted the socio-economic consequences of disrupted connectivity, especially for rural communities, women and users of essential services. ‍ The approach strengthened collaboration across DoWH and enhanced capacity to scale risk-informed infrastructure planning. Officially launched in May 2025, the Framework is being institutionalised into DoWH systems: enhancing internal planning capacity, improving risk screening processes and laying groundwork for mainstreaming resilience across PNG’s transport sector.
